opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a tricky one, and I think you have to be careful not to read too much into a single number on a leaderboard.

ARC was designed so that each task is novel. You get a handful of input–output grids, you have to infer the underlying transformation, and you apply it to a new input. In principle, memorization shouldn't help much. So when scores jump, the first question I ask is: where did the improvement come from? Is the model actually inferring new abstractions on the fly, or have we found ways to make the benchmark look more like the training distribution?

There are a few things that muddy the picture. One is the sheer amount of synthetic ARC-like data people now generate. If you procedurally create millions of grid puzzles built from the same kinds of primitives, like symmetry, object counting, gravity, and color mapping, you're effectively densifying the space around the evaluation tasks. That's legitimate engineering, but it shifts the question from "can the system generalize to something truly new?" to "how well does our prior cover the space of tasks the benchmark designers tend to write?"

The second is test-time compute. A lot of the recent gains come from sampling many candidate programs or answers, doing test-time fine-tuning on the demonstration pairs, and then verifying or voting. I actually find that interesting rather than cheating. Search plus verification is a reasonable model of what intelligence does. But it means you should report the cost. If you need thousands of samples and a lot of dollars per task, that's a very different kind of generalization than a human glancing at three examples and getting it.

So how do I assess it? A few heuristics. First, look at performance on genuinely held-out, freshly designed tasks, ideally ones created after the model and its data pipeline were frozen. The newer ARC versions were partly motivated by exactly this, because the older public sets had become saturated with community knowledge. Second, look at efficiency, not just accuracy: the accuracy-versus-compute curve tells you much more than a single point. Third, look at the failure modes. If a system nails tasks that resemble common synthetic templates but falls over on tasks requiring a slightly unusual compositional step, that's a sign it's interpolating within a learned prior rather than building new abstractions.

My overall take is that the progress is real, but it's a mix. Part of it is better priors and better search, which is a form of generalization, just not the strong, sample-efficient, human-like kind ARC was originally pointing at. Part of it is benchmark adaptation. The honest framing is that we've gotten much better at the engineering of adaptation, and the open question is whether that scales to domains where you can't cheaply generate the training distribution or verify answers. That's where I think the interesting research is. In open-ended settings, can systems discover their own curricula and abstractions rather than having us hand them the shape of the problem?

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is: it's complicated, and you have to be quite careful about what you're actually measuring.

The thing I always come back to is that ARC was designed, by François, to be a test of fluid intelligence, so the ability to take a handful of demonstration pairs, infer the underlying rule, and apply it to a novel input you've never seen. The whole premise is that the test tasks shouldn't be solvable by retrieving something from memory. So when we see a jump in scores, the first question has to be: did the system actually acquire new skills at test time, or did it just get a much better prior over the kinds of transformations that show up in the ARC distribution?

And these two things are really hard to disentangle from a leaderboard number alone. If you train on hundreds of thousands of synthetically generated ARC-like puzzles, or you use re-ARC or whatever augmentation scheme, you're essentially shifting a lot of the "generalization" burden from test time to training time. You're learning the grammar of ARC. That's a legitimate thing to do, and it clearly helps, but it's a different claim from "this model can generalize to genuinely novel structure."

So the way I personally try to assess it is along a few axes. First, how much test-time compute and test-time adaptation is involved, and what does the performance curve look like as you scale that? If a system only gets there by sampling thousands of candidate programs and doing some kind of search plus verification against the demonstration pairs, that's interesting, but it tells you the search and the verifier are doing a lot of the work, not necessarily the in-context inference. Second, I look at the gap between the public eval set and the private or semi-private sets. If that gap is large, that's a leakage or overfitting signal. Third, and this is the one I think is underrated, I look at the failure modes. Does the model fail on tasks that require composing two simple concepts it clearly gets individually? Because that compositional failure is a pretty strong sign that you have pattern matching over the training distribution rather than a flexible internal representation of the primitives.

There's also a more structural point I'd make. ARC-AGI-1 at this point has been around for a long time, people have studied it closely, and whether or not there's literal contamination, there's a kind of community-level contamination where the methods are co-evolved with the benchmark. That's partly why the newer versions were introduced, to make brute force and memorization less effective. And I think the fact that performance tends to drop sharply when you move to a fresh version is itself informative. If the capability were truly general, you'd expect a much smoother transfer.

That said, I don't want to be too dismissive. Things like test-time training, where you take a pretrained model and fine-tune it per task on augmentations of the demonstration pairs, I think that's a genuinely interesting form of generalization. It's a mechanism for acquiring a skill from very few examples. It's just that we should be precise and call it what it is. It's not the model zero-shot "understanding" the task from its weights alone, it's an adaptation procedure wrapped around the model.

So my overall view is that recent progress reflects real improvements in a kind of in-distribution-of-ARC generalization, and real improvements in search and adaptation machinery. Whether it reflects the sort of open-ended fluid intelligence that ARC was meant to probe, I think the jury's still out, and the right experiments are the ones that hold out entire concept families, not just individual tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: generalization with respect to what? ARC is designed so that each task gives you a few demonstrations, and you have to infer a rule and apply it to a new input. So progress is interesting. But a higher score alone doesn’t tell us how broadly that ability transfers.

I’d want to understand what the system has seen during training, how much development has been guided by the benchmark, and how much computation it uses at test time. There’s a difference between learning a procedure that can discover new rules and becoming very good at the particular distribution of puzzles we’ve been measuring.

One useful test would be to freeze the system and evaluate it on newly constructed tasks that introduce unfamiliar concepts or combinations of concepts. Does the improvement hold? Is it robust to changes in presentation that preserve the underlying rule?

And I wouldn’t dismiss test-time search as somehow not generalization. Search can be part of an intelligent system. But we should measure the resources it takes and be precise about the claim. Progress on ARC is evidence of a capability; it isn’t, by itself, evidence of general intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be quite careful about what you mean by generalization. ARC gives you new tasks, but a task being held out doesn’t necessarily mean that the underlying abstraction is new to the system. You might have learned a very rich set of priors that happens to cover those tasks.

That’s not to dismiss the progress. If a model can infer a transformation from a few examples and apply it correctly, that’s an interesting capability. But the score alone doesn’t tell you how it got there. How much task-specific training was involved? How much computation did it use at test time? How many candidate solutions did it generate, and how did it select among them?

I’d want to see fresh tasks, careful control over exposure to related examples, and performance broken down by the kinds of abstractions required. Can it compose familiar rules in unfamiliar ways? Does it remain reliable when you change incidental features of a task? Those tests would give me more confidence that we’re seeing transferable reasoning. A higher ARC score is evidence of progress, but the strength of the generalization claim depends on the experimental setup.
